strengths: Proposes a novel combination of kernel/GP smoothing for Neural CDE control paths with an attention-based multi-view architecture to recover information lost during smoothing.

Provides theoretical motivation linking control path regularity to NFE, showing that smoothing yields NFE scaling proportional to h^{-1} and multi-head integration is bottlenecked by the smallest bandwidth.
Empirical results on three UEA benchmarks demonstrate substantial speedups (4.3x–14.5x) and NFE reductions compared to standard spline-based Neural CDEs, with competitive or better accuracy.
Thorough ablation studies on head count, bandwidth initialization strategies (homogeneous vs. heterogeneous), and detailed computational cost breakdown (training vs. precomputation overhead).
Good reproducibility details in the appendix, including dataset descriptions, preprocessing, hyperparameter sweeps, and training settings.
weaknesses: The state-of-the-art accuracy claim is not adequately supported because the paper omits comparisons with directly related recent Neural CDE variants that it cites (e.g., Attentive NCDE, EXIT-NCDE, Neural Lad, DeNOTS), comparing only against a limited set of baselines (Linear/Cubic NCDE, ODE-RNN, GRU-D, Log-NCDE).
Evaluation is limited to regularly sampled UEA datasets; the irregular sampling and missing-data advantages of Neural CDEs are not tested, despite being a key motivation for the framework.

The theoretical analysis is informal and relies on strong assumptions (e.g., that higher-order derivatives of the latent state scale linearly with those of the control path) that are not rigorously justified; the NFE scaling theorems lack full proofs for general vector fields.

No limitations section is provided. Important practical limitations are not discussed, such as the O(N^3) scaling of exact GP inference for long sequences, hyperparameter sensitivity (bandwidth, noise variance, number of heads), and scalability to real-world irregular or noisy data.

On UWaveGestureLibrary, the proposed MVC GP has higher NFE and total time than the single-path GP, contradicting the general claim that the multi-view architecture reduces NFE; this inconsistency is not analyzed.

Presentation issues include typos (e.g., 'd_hakes', 'Bilos', 'sementicscholar'), inconsistent notation (e.g., δ appearing in some NFE bounds but not others), and missing derivation details for the heteroscedastic GP posterior used in the weighted GP paths.

strengths: Addresses a real and well-motivated bottleneck: the coupling between control-path roughness and the NFE/solver cost of Neural CDEs. The framing that interpolation precision drives stiffness is coherent and useful.

The core remedy (replacing exact interpolation with Kernel/GP smoothing to decouple integration cost from input noise) is sensible, and the reported NFE reductions are large and consistent across all three datasets (e.g., ~633 -> ~95 on CharacterTrajectories, ~4340 -> ~219 on UWave).
The Multi-View/Multi-View-Convolutional attention mechanism (MV-CDE/MVC-CDE) is a reasonable architectural extension, and the ablations over head count and bandwidth provide some practical insight.
The appendix documents hyperparameters, splits, preprocessing, and per-dataset solver tolerances, which partially supports reproducibility.
The noise-robustness sweep is a reasonable additional analysis and the qualitative attention visualizations are informative.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'state-of-the-art accuracy' is not supported. The paper uses a non-standard 60/20/20 split instead of the standard UEA train/test splits, so results cannot be compared to any published SOTA. Moreover, the reported Linear/Cubic Neural CDE accuracies (e.g., 85.6%/86.6% on CharacterTrajectories, 83.9%/84.8% on UWave) are far below those commonly reported in the Neural CDE literature (~98%/~96%), strongly suggesting the baselines are undertuned or the pipeline is misconfigured. This undermines the validity of every comparison in the paper.

The theoretical results are informal and oversimplified. Theorem 3.1 asserts ||d^{p+1}z/dt^{p+1}|| ∝ ||d^{p+1}X/dt^{p+1}|| without justification; the higher derivatives of the solution depend on derivatives of f and products of state/control terms, not a simple proportionality. The 'proofs' in Appendix A.1-A.3 rely on loose heuristics presented as theorems.

Appendix A.5 claims GP provides a 'strictly more accurate' reconstruction than kernel smoothing, but this holds only under the assumed GP prior (i.e., it is circular) and is contradicted by the paper's own single-path experiments, where kernel smoothing beats GP on 2 of 3 datasets (89.20 vs 88.15; 96.32 vs 96.12). This inconsistency is never acknowledged.

The multi-scale motivation is inconsistent with the reported results. The best MVC-CDE (GP) configurations use homogeneous bandwidths on 2 of 3 datasets (e.g., [166.6,166.6,166.6,166.6] and [91.0,91.0,91.0]), directly contradicting the claim that scale diversity is essential and the Appendix C.3 claim that heterogeneous bandwidths are superior.

Theorem 3.4 states that adding a head with small h increases total NFE (bottlenecked by min h), yet the paper does not reconcile this with the empirical claim that more heads help; the 'temporal parallelization' interpretation is a reframing rather than a demonstrated mechanism.

Efficiency is only benchmarked against CDE variants. Simple baselines such as GRU-D are far faster (e.g., 10.56s vs 22.63s on CharacterTrajectories) and nearly as accurate, so the practical 'scalable time-series modeling' claim is weaker than presented.

Novelty is limited: the effect of path roughness/interpolation on NFE is well documented (e.g., Morrill et al., 2022), and smoothing the control path is a fairly direct remedy; the attention-based recovery is incremental relative to existing Attentive NCDEs, which are cited but not compared against.
There is no explicit limitations section despite strong headline claims, and no code release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility and the ability of others to build on the work.

Presentation issues: informal 'theorems' presented as established results, notation errors (e.g., 'd_hakes'), a figure caption that does not match its content (Figure 1), and reference formatting problems.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem identification: the paper correctly isolates the NFE/solver-stiffness bottleneck of Neural CDEs and links it to the roughness of the driving control path, a genuinely practical issue for continuous-time sequence models.

Novel and sensible methodological idea: replacing exact spline interpolation with Kernel/GP smoothing to decouple integration cost from input noise, combined with an attention-based Multi-View (MV-CDE/MVC-CDE) mechanism to recover detail lost to over-smoothing. The Q-Former-inspired weighting of the GP noise covariance by attention scores is a neat construction.

Reasonable theoretical framing: the paper attempts to connect Sobolev-type regularity of the control path to solver step size (Theorems 3.1-3.2, Corollaries 3.3-3.4) and derives explicit complexity contrasts between splines (NFE scaling with finite differences) and smoothing (NFE ∝ h^{-1}). The direction of the argument is correct even if loose.

Consistent empirical gains: MVC-CDE (GP) achieves the best accuracy on all three benchmarks (e.g., 95.07% vs 86.61% cubic on CharacterTrajectories; 98.28% on SpokenArabicDigits; 95.39% on UWaveGestureLibrary) with reported 5-14x wall-clock speedups over spline-based CDEs and large NFE reductions.

Thorough supplementary analysis: head-count and bandwidth ablations, noise-robustness sweeps, attention heatmaps, and a granular cost breakdown (pre-computation vs iterative training) support the narrative and are informative.
Good reproducibility: dataset splits, normalization, optimizer settings, solver tolerances, and per-dataset hyperparameters (bandwidths, lengthscales, noise) are reported in detail.
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scope relative to the strong claims: only three UEA datasets are used, yet the paper repeatedly claims 'state-of-the-art.' This is thin evidence for a SOTA assertion, and the selection (CharacterTrajectories, SpokenArabicDigits, UWaveGestureLibrary) may not represent the broader irregular/medical regimes the motivation emphasizes.

Missing directly relevant baselines: Attentive NCDEs (Jhin et al., 2024), ContiFormer, Neural RDE (Morrill et al., 2021), Neural Lad, and EXIT-NCDE are cited and discussed but never compared. Not benchmarking against the most similar attention-based CDE undercuts both the novelty and the SOTA claim.

The practical efficiency motivation is partially undercut: GRU-D attains competitive accuracy (93.17 vs 95.07 on CharacterTrajectories; 96.57 vs 98.28 on SpokenArabicDigits; 78.86 vs 95.39 on UWave) at a small fraction of the time (e.g., 2.02s vs 7.32s on SpokenArabicDigits) with zero NFE. The claimed advantages are therefore relative to other CDEs, not to fast discrete baselines, which weakens the 'practical applicability' argument.

Theory is loose/informal: Theorem 3.1 is explicitly labeled informal and its proof assumes bounded/Lipschitz vector fields to claim ||z^{(p+1)}|| ∝ ||X^{(p+1)}||, which is only approximate for the multiplicative f(z)dX/dt dynamics. The proof of Theorem 3.2 conflates a bound on kernel derivatives with a bound on the smoothed path derivatives and yields a worst-case bound independent of the data noise, so it does not rigorously establish the claimed noise-decoupling.

Internal inconsistencies and presentation issues: the abstract claims reductions in 'total inference time' whereas the reported metric is total wall-clock (trajectory fit + training + evaluation), i.e., largely a training-time metric. Additionally, the 'Main' MVC-GP configurations use homogeneous bandwidths (e.g., [166.6,166.6,166.6,166.6]), which contradicts the heterogeneous multi-scale diversity argument advanced in the ablation (Appendix C.3).

Unresolved tension in the multi-view design: Theorem 3.4 states total NFE is bottlenecked by min_m h_m, which appears to conflict with the goal of adding small-h heads to recover high-frequency detail; the paper acknowledges this as a 'critical design choice' but does not resolve or empirically quantify how the ensemble avoids paying the smallest-h cost.

The claim that attention 'recovers high-frequency information' is supported only qualitatively via attention heatmaps; no quantitative analysis (e.g., reconstruction error vs bandwidth/heads, spectral analysis) demonstrates actual information recovery.
No code/artifact release is mentioned, and the theoretical claims rely on appendix material whose proofs are sketched rather than fully developed.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: identifies path roughness from exact interpolation of noisy observations as a key driver of high NFE in Neural CDEs, and provides an intuitive theoretical link between NFE and control-path derivatives.

Proposes a practical smoothing-based path construction (kernel and GP smoothing) and a multi-view attention architecture (MV-CDE/MVC-CDE) that parallelizes integration across multiple smoothed trajectories, addressing the solver-stiffness bottleneck directly.

Empirical results on three UEA benchmarks show substantial NFE and training-time reductions over spline-based Neural CDEs. For example, on UWaveGestureLibrary MVC GP uses 219 NFE vs. 1042 for cubic NCDE and trains in 12.3s vs. 81.8s, while improving accuracy (95.39% vs. 85.68%). Similar gains are shown on SpokenArabicDigits and CharacterTrajectories.

Noise robustness experiments and ablations (head count, bandwidth initialization, solver order, irregular-sampling drop rates) provide useful practical insights and support the central claim that smoothing stabilizes solver behavior under noisy inputs.

The limitations section is honest and identifies important drawbacks, including solver dependency, bandwidth sensitivity, the stiffest-head bottleneck, and potential loss of high-frequency information.
The paper provides extensive hyperparameter settings, dataset descriptions, and training details in the appendix, and uses public datasets, making the work reasonably reproducible in principle.
No ethical concerns are apparent; the work advances efficient continuous-time sequence modeling with no obvious harmful applications.
weaknesses: The state-of-the-art accuracy claim is not supported across all benchmarks. On CharacterTrajectories, Mamba achieves 96.64% versus MVC GP's 95.07%, and GRU-D achieves 93.17% while being much faster. The abstract's claim of 'state-of-the-art accuracy' is therefore an overstatement.

Efficiency claims are also overstated. NFE reductions relative to cubic spline CDEs are roughly 2.5x-4.8x, not an order of magnitude; speedups vary by dataset and baseline, and the strongest speedups are against weaker or slower baselines rather than the best-performing spline methods.

The experimental protocol deviates from standard UEA train/test splits by using a 60/20/20 re-split. This makes reported accuracies incomparable to published UEA results and weakens the SOTA comparison. No code is released.

The irregular-sampling evaluation is unclear and potentially invalid. The preprocessing states that time is defined as regular intervals t in {0,...,T} with dt=1. If missing observations are dropped and then reindexed, the method is not actually tested on irregular timestamps, undermining the claimed robustness to missing/irregular data. Actual timestamp handling and gap treatment are not described.

The theoretical analysis is heuristic rather than rigorous. Theorem 3.1 asserts that NFE depends only on derivatives of the control path, but adaptive solver error also depends on the vector field f and the solution derivatives. The assumed proportionality between state derivatives and control-path derivatives is not justified for nonlinear f, and the Nadaraya-Watson/GP derivative bound can fail near boundaries or data gaps. Corollary 3.3's h^{-1} scaling is also loose for large h.

Novelty is incremental. Kernel/GP smoothing of control paths is a natural idea, and the multi-view architecture is essentially an ensemble of CDEs with different smoothing bandwidths plus Q-Former-style attention. The paper does not adequately distinguish itself from prior work on interpolation choices for Neural CDEs (e.g., Morrill et al., 2022) beyond citation, and the main-text empirical comparison omits a direct smoothing-spline baseline, which appears only in the appendix.

Experimental scope is limited: only three small classification datasets in the main text, one forecasting dataset with a single horizon, no large-scale long-sequence benchmarks, and no statistical significance tests. The forecasting setup uses a simple linear head and may not validate broader generative capabilities.

Attention/interpretability analysis is qualitative. The paper claims that heads capture distinct temporal patterns, but quantitative evidence is limited to diversity metrics in the appendix; there is no task-relevant evaluation of whether the recovered multi-view information is actually meaningful.

Presentation issues include typos and inconsistencies: 'd_haldon' in the latent state dimension, 'sementicscholar' in references, Eq. 4 uses k_h instead of k_{h_m}, 'KS' is not defined in the main text, and the number of heads M is not consistently reported across experiments.

GP smoothing is non-causal and requires O(N^3) preprocessing, which limits streaming and long-sequence applicability. Although the authors acknowledge this and suggest rolling causal windows, the main text does not benchmark the latency or overhead of that causal approximation.

Baseline fairness is imperfect. Capacity matching is applied to Linear/Cubic NCDEs but not to all baselines (e.g., Mamba, GRU-D), and solver tolerance tuning is not uniform across all methods, which may affect the Pareto comparisons.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: the computational inefficiency of Neural CDEs caused by solver stiffness from rough control paths.
Proposes a simple, intuitive solution: replacing exact interpolation with kernel or Gaussian Process smoothing to decouple integration cost from input noise.
Provides theoretical scaling laws (Theorems 3.1–3.4) linking path regularity to NFE, offering useful qualitative insights even if the proofs are heuristic.
Introduces a novel multi-view attention architecture (MV-CDE, MVC-CDE) inspired by Q-Former to recover information lost during smoothing.
Empirical results show substantial reductions in NFE and training time (4×–16× speedup) on three UEA datasets.
Extensive appendix with ablations on head count, bandwidth initialization, solver order, noise robustness, irregular sampling, high-dimensional scalability, and comparison with smoothing splines.
Includes an honest limitations section that acknowledges solver dependency, bandwidth sensitivity, the stiffest-head bottleneck, and frequency information loss.
weaknesses: Theoretical claims are not rigorously established. Theorem 3.1 assumes proportionality between derivatives of the latent state z and the control path X without justification; the NFE bounds use '≲' and ignore constants; the proofs in Appendix A are sketchy (e.g., Theorem 3.2's proof for GP posterior mean is hand-wavy, and the step-size control derivation ignores the mixed relative/absolute error norms used in practice).

The state-of-the-art accuracy claim is overstated. On CharacterTrajectories, Mamba achieves 96.64% vs. MVC GP's 95.07%. Only three datasets are evaluated for main classification, and there is no comparison to many recent CDE variants (e.g., Attentive NCDEs, EXIT-NCDE, Neural Lad) or strong time-series classification baselines.

The benefit of the multi-view mechanism is not clearly isolated. The best MVC GP model uses homogeneous bandwidths (e.g., all 166.6 for CharacterTrajectories, all 91.0 for SpokenArabicDigits), contradicting the claim that multiple temporal scales are necessary. The improvement over single-path GP appears to come largely from the CNN feature extractor and attention, not from multi-scale smoothing.

The computational cost of GP smoothing during integration is not analyzed. Evaluating the GP posterior mean at arbitrary t requires O(N²) per solver step; for long sequences this could be significant. The paper claims a one-time preprocessing cost but does not specify how the path is evaluated during integration (e.g., precomputed grid vs. on-the-fly), raising reproducibility concerns.

Efficiency comparisons may be unfair. Baselines use natural cubic splines, but other interpolation schemes (e.g., Hermite splines) might be more efficient; solver tolerances were tuned for baselines but perhaps not optimally; the reported total time includes trajectory fitting, yet the cost of per-sequence GP matrix inversion (O(N³)) is not fully accounted for in the complexity discussion.

The forecasting experiment is weak. Only one dataset (ETTm1) is used, the improvement over GRU is modest (MSE 0.428 vs. 0.476), and there is no comparison to state-of-the-art forecasting models such as Informer or Autoformer.

Presentation issues undermine clarity: inconsistent naming (MVC-CDE vs. MVC GP), typos (e.g., 'd_haldon' instead of d_hidden), future references (e.g., 2026) that appear erroneous, and claims like 'performing competitively alongside Mamba' that are not fully supported by the reported numbers.

The novelty of explicit path smoothing is questionable. Prior work (e.g., Morrill et al., 2022) discusses interpolation schemes for Neural CDEs, and smoothing splines are a standard technique. The attention mechanism is borrowed from Q-Former, making the contribution incremental.

The 'parallel integration' does not actually parallelize computation; it concatenates states into a single larger ODE system. The reported NFE is for the combined system and is only low because very large bandwidths are used, which may limit expressiveness.
The method introduces additional hyperparameters (bandwidth h, number of heads M) that require tuning, adding practical complexity and sensitivity not fully addressed in the experiments.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and under-appreciated bottleneck in Neural CDEs: the NFE cost is governed by the geometric roughness of the control path rather than the learned vector field. This framing is clear and useful, and the proposed remedy (explicit path smoothing with Kernel/GP priors) follows naturally from it.

The theoretical scaffolding (Theorems 3.1, 3.2, Corollary 3.3, Theorem 3.4) provides an intuitive and coherent link between path regularity (derivative bounds scaling as h^-p), NFE, and the multi-head bottleneck. While heuristic, it gives practitioners actionable guidance (NFE ~ delta^-1/(p+1) h^-1).

The empirical study is broad: NFE, wall-clock time, noise robustness, head-count ablation, solver-order analysis, high-dimensional (PEMS-SF, 963 dims), irregular-sampling robustness, and memory/compute breakdowns. The NFE reductions (e.g., UWave Cubic ~1042 vs MVC GP ~218) and the noise-robustness results (NFE nearly constant under added noise) convincingly support the central efficiency claim.

The multi-view attention design (learnable queries over smoothed paths, with a convolutional front-end for context) is a sensible adaptation of Q-Former-style querying to the CDE setting, and the block-diagonal parallel integration is a clean way to share solver cost.

The paper is generally well-organized, the limitations section is honest (solver dependence, bandwidth tuning, stiffest-head bottleneck, frequency loss), and the appendices provide substantial reproducibility detail (splits, hyperparameters, capacity matching).
weaknesses: The theoretical claims are heuristic rather than rigorous. Theorem 3.1 is essentially standard ODE step-size control with a proportionality assumption (||d^{p+1}z|| proportional to ||d^{p+1}X||) that is asserted, not proven, and the constant in the bound hides dependencies on the vector field. The 'theorem' label overstates the rigor.

Baseline tuning is questionable. On CharacterTrajectories, Cubic CDE reaches only 91.89% and GRU-D (93.17%) outperforms it, while single-path GP (88.15%) is worse than both; these CDE numbers are far below what is typically reported for this benchmark. Since all baselines are self-implemented and capacity-matched rather than compared to published results, the 'SOTA accuracy' claim is not well established. Mamba also beats MVC-CDE on CharacterTrajectories (96.64 vs 95.07).

The marginal benefit of the multi-view attention mechanism is modest and sometimes within noise (e.g., MV GP 92.95±1.24 vs GP 91.14±1.87 on UWave; MV GP 97.52±0.39 vs GP 96.12±0.33 on SpokenArabicDigits). The claim that the attention mechanism 'recovers lost details' rests on relatively small deltas.

There is an internal inconsistency: the main configuration of MVC GP uses homogeneous bandwidths for CharacterTrajectories and SpokenArabicDigits ([166.6,...] and [91.0,91.0,91.0]) while Appendix C.2 argues heterogeneous bandwidths are superior. The paper does not reconcile why the best models use the supposedly inferior configuration.

GP smoothing is O(N^3) per trajectory and is a per-sample preprocessing cost that is not amortized across batches; for long sequences this could dominate. The 'online/streaming' applicability is only weakly supported—the paper concedes global GP/kernel smoothing is offline and relies on rolling-window fitting without a rigorous latency analysis.

The forecasting evaluation (Table 1) is a single dataset (ETTm1) with one horizon, and the causal/streaming argument is mostly assertion. The attention interpretability analysis (Section 4.6) is qualitative and dataset-anecdotal.

Minor presentation issues: typographical/notation errors (e.g., 'd_haldon', 'Concat', inconsistent use of Concat vs concat, 'Multi-Model Attention' figure title), and the single-path smoothing baselines are sometimes weaker than non-smooth baselines, which complicates the narrative.
